name: Yusuf Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead four dispatch clerks on an evening shift at a large parcel company. We take the bags the drivers could not fit, check the van sheets and call customers when a parcel is truly missing. I moved up from the service counter after it closed, so I am a junior lead and still learning the route board. I have a bachelor's degree, but I am slower at planning than the other leads and have never used an AI tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you go home to after that shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and live with my partner Rina, who works paid shifts at a laundrette. Our daughter and son are grown and live separately. We rent, my lead pay is low for this job, and we have about three weeks of expenses saved; there are few similar posts nearby. Retirement is somewhere ahead, but I do not know the pension amount or when I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software stays small, parcels still miss their vans and I still have to sort out the handover. The company has cut our paid late shift twice this month, though. Rina and I have only about three weeks of expenses saved, so I think about the rent before I think about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my four dispatch clerks to keep the signed van sheet for every missed bag. I'd tell the depot manager that moving the late shift earlier does not make the last van arrive earlier. I would not praise a new tool I have never opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came into this lead job recently from a long stretch at the service counter, and I'm still slower at the route board than the other leads. My bachelor's degree is old and doesn't make the rent smaller. With few similar management jobs nearby, losing paid late hours is already a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This Friday I'll match the seven bags marked late with the drivers' signed van sheets and send the corrected list to the depot manager. I'll keep the paper handover board in the first plateau year and stop buying lunch at the depot for two months, taking food from home instead. I'll ask payroll for the exact lost late-shift pay before deciding whether any extra cash can be saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. The rent date is the same even when the late shift ends early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you move into the lead post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service counter closed and this was the paid opening I could reach by bus. I know what a customer needs when a parcel is lost, but managing four route clerks is newer to me. I don't want to pretend I am the best lead in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter and son are grown and have homes of their own. They visit and bring food sometimes, but I have not asked them to pay our rent. I would speak to Rina before asking either child for money.

say: I'd tell clerks to keep **signed van sheets** for missed bags.
I'd tell the depot manager the **late shift** still needs a real handover.
think: My **new lead role** and scarce local jobs make lost hours worrying.
Three weeks saved will not cover many **rent dates**.
do: Match **seven late bags** to signed van sheets this Friday.
Keep the **paper handover board** through the first plateau year.
Bring **lunch from home** for two months while late-shift pay is reduced.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent and lost paid hours.
S0.quote: The rent date is the same even when the late shift ends early.
fieldNote: The paid late-shift cut creates **present income risk** in a plateau.
He is a **recent junior lead**, skilled at customer problems but still learning route planning.
He does not assume **adult children** can pay rent.

steps.text: Match seven late parcels to signed van sheets this Friday
Bring lunch from home for two months while paid late hours remain cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking vans, checking scans, writing handover notes and answering missing-parcel calls take most of my shift. A stronger system could do those jobs while the drivers still carry the bags. My four-clerk desk could become one person on exceptions, and I am a new lead rather than the one who built the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the depot manager to show the clerks the new staffing rota before changing anyone's hours. I'd ask for a test on last month's missed bags, not a sales demonstration. I would tell customers a human phone number is still needed for a parcel that never reached a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose the lead allowance and be sent back to a lower paid desk, or lose the desk entirely. I have never used AI and I would not catch a bad route suggestion without training. Rina's laundrette pay covers some groceries, not our rent, and three weeks saved will disappear quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'll ask the manager for a paid old-case test with an experienced route clerk beside me, only if the company approves the time. I'll keep checking signed van sheets while the results are reviewed and request the next rota in writing. I'll apply for posted local dispatch work only where the wage and bus hours can cover our rent and food, leaving this job only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my pay and the little time we have to search. I can ask for a test, but I cannot order the company to keep four clerks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the old-case test show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seven bags that were loaded onto the wrong van are a good start. If the system says they arrived because a scan was repeated, I need the driver sheet to prove otherwise. A repeated scan is not a delivered parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If an experienced clerk offers paid instruction and shows me the source scans, yes. I am slow at new screens; I have not used AI, and I won't teach myself on a live customer's lost parcel. I would not press the live button without approval.

say: I'd ask for a **written staffing rota** before hours change.
I'd ask for **old missed-bag testing** and a human customer line.
think: I could lose my **lead allowance or desk** in this change.
Rina's pay cannot cover rent, and **three weeks cash** would vanish quickly.
do: Request a **paid missed-bag test** only with company approval and experienced clerk beside me.
Keep checking **signed van sheets** while test results are reviewed.
Apply for **posted local dispatch work** only with viable pay and bus hours; leave after signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own pay and search time.
S1.quote: A repeated scan is not a delivered parcel.
fieldNote: The same seven bags test whether AI mistakes **duplicate scans** for deliveries.
He is willing to learn only with **offered paid instruction** and source scans.
A posted job needs **affordable pay** and workable bus hours before he applies.

steps.text: Request paid missed-bag test only with company approval and experienced clerk
Keep checking signed van sheets while test results are reviewed
Apply for posted dispatch jobs with viable pay and bus hours; leave only after signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 full AGI could plan the routes, answer missing-parcel calls and check handovers better and cheaper than our desk. The drivers and sorters still lift bags until capable robots arrive around 2031, but their schedules and scan decisions change in 2028. My knees are not good enough for a full sorting shift without checking it with a clinician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the clerks to ask for written notice terms now, not wait for a locked screen. I'd tell Rina we should stop the planned sofa payment and keep the rent money in the bank. I'd tell our children what is happening without asking them to promise support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior lead post to end, and perhaps the whole dispatch desk. Rina's laundrette wage alone cannot cover rent and bills; three weeks of cash would go before another local management post appears. I'd be awake counting the days to rent and wondering whether I can work enough years for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask human resources for written notice and severance figures and cancel the sofa order before its payment is due. If AGI arrives in 2028 and the desk ends, I'll apply for posted local work only after checking its pay, bus journey and my ability to do the physical tasks; I would accept only if wages with Rina's confirmed hours cover rent, food and medicine. I'd check public help eligibility and apply only if we qualify, and ask the landlord about a payment plan before rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. Three weeks is not a bridge from a lost wage to an unknown pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would loading parcels be a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can lift a small bag, but a full shift on concrete floors hurts my knees. I'd ask my clinician what work is safe and look at actual job duties before applying. The physical sorting jobs themselves face capable robots around 2031, so they may only buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old would you be then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty in 2028. I don't know what pension I could draw or when; I need the plan statement, not a guess. Our children are adults, and I will not put their wages in our budget.

say: I'd ask for **written notice and severance** figures.
I'd tell Rina the **sofa payment** must stop before it is due.
think: I expect my **junior lead wage** to end by 2028.
Three weeks cash and Rina's pay cannot bridge **rent to retirement**.
do: Request **written notice terms** and cancel the sofa order before payment.
Apply for **posted local work** only after checking pay, bus route and physical fitness; accept if combined wages cover essentials.
Check **public help eligibility** before applying if the desk ends.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss and a short rent clock.
S2.quote: Three weeks is not a bridge from a lost wage to an unknown pension.
fieldNote: He refuses to assume **pension eligibility** at sixty.
Knee pain limits the supposed **physical sorting fallback** even before 2031 robots.
He seeks public aid only after **checking eligibility**.

steps.text: Cancel sofa order before payment comes due
Apply for local jobs after pay, bus and health checks; accept only with affordable combined wages
Check public help eligibility and apply only if household qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three in 2031, I might still need wages and cannot count on an unknown pension. Dispatch planning faces AGI then, while the drivers' and sorters' hands face capable robots around 2034. Five years gives me time to get real figures, not a guarantee that my knees or this depot last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for its staffing dates and an honest pension statement. I'd tell Rina we should know our rent and medicine costs before any talk of stopping work. I'd tell our children we are making a plan, not asking them for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still be paid as a junior lead for a few years, which matters. I don't know whether I have enough pension to retire at sixty-three, and our small cash cushion makes early exit dangerous. A posted local job might pay less, but I could compare it while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'll request a written pension estimate with the earliest eligible date and expected amount, and compare it with rent, food and medicine. I'd save 20 weekly if both wages cover those bills, aiming for one month of expenses without claiming I can reach it quickly. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for posted local work with bus access only if its wage and Rina's confirmed pay cover essentials; I would leave the depot only after a signed offer or confirmed pension income that truly covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not ready to stop work. Five years lets me check the paper, but it does not deposit money for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension estimate is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep working if a paid post exists and my health permits. I would not call a small pension statement a retirement plan. We would ask about help only if eligible, not assume it is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your son for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would speak with Rina first, and I wouldn't build our regular rent around our son's goodwill. He has his own household. If we had a one-off emergency, I might ask whether he can afford a small loan, with repayment agreed, but not without his consent.

say: I'd ask for a **written pension estimate** and staffing dates.
I'd tell our children we are **not budgeting their wages**.
think: I may need **paid work at sixty-three** if pension income falls short.
A local opening may pay less, but I can **compare offers while employed**.
do: Request a **pension estimate** with eligible date and amount in 2027.
Save **20 weekly** only while both wages cover rent, food and medicine.
Apply for **posted bus-accessible work** after 2031 only with affordable confirmed pay; leave after signed offer or sufficient pension.
feel: I feel **anxious** about uncertain pension income.
S3.quote: I would not call a small pension statement a retirement plan.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **pension estimate** from money available to spend.
The 20 weekly transfer depends on **both wages** covering essentials.
He would **consult Rina** before asking their son for a loan; taking it requires his agreement and repayment terms.

steps.text: Request written pension estimate with earliest eligible date and expected amount in 2027
Save 20 weekly only while both wages cover rent, food and medicine
Apply for bus-accessible jobs; leave only after affordable signed offer or sufficient confirmed pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight in 2036. Our children will still be adults with lives of their own, and I cannot say what our rent or pension will be. Dispatch plans face AGI in 2036, and physical sorting faces capable robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to give older staff written dates for any desk changes. I'd tell Rina we should compare a pension statement with the actual rent every year. I'd tell our children we can talk about the future without asking them to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might bring me to retirement, but I cannot promise it without the pension amount and eligibility date. I could keep earning in dispatch for some of those years, build a little cash and then see what is available. I am worried about being sixty-eight with only rent receipts and no paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll request the pension provider's written eligibility date and projected monthly amount, and review it with Rina against our rent, food and medicine. I'll put 30 weekly into cash only if both paychecks cover those costs, stopping if Rina's hours fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stop working only if actual pension income and Rina's confirmed pay cover essentials; otherwise I'd apply for posted local work that fits my health and bus travel, accepting only a wage that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the unknown figure, even with ten years to ask. The pension letter has to be worth more than the paper it is printed on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move nearer your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess. They live in different places and have their own rent to pay. I would need a real affordable home, Rina's agreement and a paid job or pension that covers living costs before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your knees worsen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a clinician about safe duties before applying for physical work. I can manage a route board if the job exists, but I cannot count on carrying parcels at sixty-eight. A pension that does not cover medicine is not a retirement date.

say: I'd ask for **written desk-change dates** for older staff.
I'd tell Rina to compare **pension and rent** each year.
think: Retirement may be possible only with **real eligibility** and enough income.
I worry about being sixty-eight without **adequate pension** or paid work.
do: Request **pension eligibility and amount** this winter and compare it with essentials.
Save **30 weekly** only while both paychecks cover rent, food and medicine; stop if Rina's hours fall.
Apply for **local work** only if pension plus Rina's confirmed pay fall short, duties fit health, bus accessible and pay covers bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the pension figure despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: A pension that does not cover medicine is not a retirement date.
fieldNote: He makes retirement conditional on **actual pension** and partner pay covering essentials.
Health and bus access constrain **later job choices**.
He will not assume adult children can **fund or house** him.

steps.text: Request written pension eligibility and projected monthly amount; compare with rent, food and medicine
Save 30 weekly only while both wages cover essentials; stop if Rina’s hours fall
Apply for local work if pension plus Rina's confirmed pay insufficient; accept safe bus-accessible affordable job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My dispatch desk could end at sixty with three weeks' savings, and I do not know my pension date or amount. Written notice, help eligibility I can verify and a real paid job reachable by bus would help. I need pay that covers rent, food and medicine, not a new title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a late bag gets to an older person who cannot travel to the depot. I can correct a van sheet, but I still need a driver to carry the parcel. A tracking mark does not knock on a door.

headlineQuote: A tracking mark does not knock on a door.
portrait: Yusuf, **58**, is a recent junior lead of four parcel-dispatch clerks after years at a service counter.
He has a bachelor's degree, is **still learning route planning**, and has never used AI.
Low pay, lost late shifts, **three weeks saved** and few nearby posts make rent hard to protect.
He seeks **real pension figures** and bus-accessible paid work without assuming his grown children will fund him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his dispatch desk before he knows his pension eligibility or amount.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice** and verified public help eligibility.
He needs a **bus-accessible paid job** covering rent, food and medicine.
